# trust_region_least_squares - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/trust-region-least-squares/^0.9/

## Expand description

A dense trust-region-reflective (TRF) nonlinear least-squares solver that
reproduces [ scipy.optimize.least_squares](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.optimize.least_squares.html) (

`method='trf'`, 2-point
Jacobian) bit-for-bit. It covers SciPy’s dense unbounded path for arbitrary
problem dimension `n` and every SciPy loss (`linear`, `soft_l1`, `huber`,
`cauchy`, `arctan`) with the `f_scale` robust-reweighting parameter; see
[Scope](https://docs.rs#scope)for the supported dimensionality.

It is built to be a general-purpose solver, not a one-off port: give it a
residual `r: R^n -> R^m` and a starting point and it runs the same
trust-region Newton iteration SciPy does, down to the last bit. The
linear-algebra
operations that determine the last bits of the trajectory – the thin SVD of
the scaled Jacobian and the small BLAS reductions around it – are *injected*
through the [ trf::ThinSvd](https://docs.rs/trf/trait.ThinSvd.html) trait. Supplying an implementation backed by a
host LAPACK/BLAS (see the optional

`hostlapack` module) lets the solver
reproduce that backend’s numerical trajectory exactly, which is what makes
bit-for-bit agreement with a pinned SciPy/NumPy runtime achievable rather
than merely tolerance-close.Use it when you need scipy-identical least-squares results in Rust: porting a Python pipeline, cross-checking a Rust solver against SciPy, or pinning a numerical result so it cannot silently drift between language runtimes.

[§](https://docs.rs#scope)Scope

- `trf`- `scipy.optimize._lsq.trf.trf_no_bounds`, with the injectable- `trf::ThinSvd`- `loss`/- `f_scale`robust path. Ships the default in-crate- `trf::NalgebraThinSvd`- `trf::trf_solve`] entry point so the solver runs out of the box.
- `model`- `model::ResidualModel`- `model::solve_model`
- `data`- `data::BuiltinResidual`- `data::DataProblem`- `data::solve_data_problem`
- `batch`- `batch::solve_drop_one`- `batch::solve_perturbed`- `rayon`pool, with per-index results bit-identical to the equivalent serial solve. Serial leave-one-out twins (- `batch::solve_drop_one_serial`- `wasm32`consumers the same report without rayon.
- `loss`- `construct_loss_function`+- `IMPLEMENTED_LOSSES`) and- `scale_for_robust_loss_function`, reproduced bit-for-bit.
- `numdiff`- `_numdiff.approx_derivative(..., method="2-point")`path.
- `parity`
- `hostlapack`- `trf::ThinSvd`

The iteration is general in `n`: give it a residual `r: R^n -> R^m` for any
`n >= 1` (with `m >= n` for the dense exact trust-region solve) and it runs
SciPy’s `trf_no_bounds` trajectory bit-for-bit. All five SciPy losses are
supported at every dimension. Bit-exact parity is enforced by committed
fixtures across `n` in {2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8} times each loss; see the
`fixtures-generators` directory and the `tests` suite.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

The solver runs out of the box: hand [ model::solve_model](https://docs.rs/model/fn.solve_model.html) a residual model
and a starting point and it drives the trust-region iteration through the
default in-crate SVD. This fits the overdetermined system whose
least-squares solution is

`[1.0, 2.0]`:```
use trust_region_least_squares::model::{solve_model, ResidualModel};
use trust_region_least_squares::trf::TrfOptions;
// r(x) = [x0 - 1, x1 - 2, x0 + x1 - 3]; minimized at x = [1, 2].
struct Consistent;
impl ResidualModel for Consistent {
    fn residual(&self, x: &[f64], out: &mut Vec<f64>) {
        out.clear();
        out.push(x[0] - 1.0);
        out.push(x[1] - 2.0);
        out.push(x[0] + x[1] - 3.0);
    }
    // The Jacobian defaults to the bit-exact 2-point finite difference.
}
let result = solve_model(&Consistent, &[0.0, 0.0], &TrfOptions::default())
    .expect("solve");
assert!(result.success());
assert!((result.x[0] - 1.0).abs() < 1e-6);
assert!((result.x[1] - 2.0).abs() < 1e-6);
```
The thin SVD is still an injectable seam. The default
[ trf::NalgebraThinSvd](https://docs.rs/trf/struct.NalgebraThinSvd.html) is a legitimate independent SVD but is

*not*bit-identical to a pinned SciPy/NumPy runtime; for bit-for-bit parity inject the

[backend (the](https://docs.rs/hostlapack/struct.LapackSvd.html)

`hostlapack::LapackSvd``*_with` entry points take a
[). The iteration is identical, only the SVD/BLAS seam changes.](https://docs.rs/trf/trait.ThinSvd.html)

`trf::ThinSvd`## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [batch](https://docs.rs/batch/index.html)
- Parallel leave-one-out and multi-start re-solves.
- [data](https://docs.rs/data/index.html)
- Data-driven built-in residuals: the path a host-language binding drives without ever re-entering the host language inside the solver loop.
- [hostlapack](https://docs.rs/hostlapack/index.html)
- Host LAPACK and BLAS bridge for pinned SciPy 1.18.0 parity runs.

- [model](https://docs.rs/model/index.html)
- A Rust-side residual model, so the residual, its Jacobian, and any per-evaluation corrections live in Rust instead of behind a closure boundary supplied by the caller.
- [numdiff](https://docs.rs/numdiff/index.html)

- [parity](https://docs.rs/parity/index.html)

- [trf](https://docs.rs/trf/index.html)
- Dense unbounded trust-region reflective least-squares matching
`scipy.optimize._lsq.trf.trf_no_bounds`for arbitrary problem dimension`n`.

# approx - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/approx/^0.5/

## Expand description

A crate that provides facilities for testing the approximate equality of floating-point based types, using either relative difference, or units in the last place (ULPs) comparisons.

You can also use the `*_{eq, ne}!` and `assert_*_{eq, ne}!` macros to test for equality using a
more positional style:

```
#[macro_use]
extern crate approx;
use std::f64;
abs_diff_eq!(1.0, 1.0);
abs_diff_eq!(1.0, 1.0, epsilon = f64::EPSILON);
relative_eq!(1.0, 1.0);
relative_eq!(1.0, 1.0, epsilon = f64::EPSILON);
relative_eq!(1.0, 1.0, max_relative = 1.0);
relative_eq!(1.0, 1.0, epsilon = f64::EPSILON, max_relative = 1.0);
relative_eq!(1.0, 1.0, max_relative = 1.0, epsilon = f64::EPSILON);
ulps_eq!(1.0, 1.0);
ulps_eq!(1.0, 1.0, epsilon = f64::EPSILON);
ulps_eq!(1.0, 1.0, max_ulps = 4);
ulps_eq!(1.0, 1.0, epsilon = f64::EPSILON, max_ulps = 4);
ulps_eq!(1.0, 1.0, max_ulps = 4, epsilon = f64::EPSILON);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-approximate-equality-for-custom-types)Implementing approximate equality for custom types

The `*Eq` traits allow approximate equalities to be implemented on types, based on the
fundamental floating point implementations.

For example, we might want to be able to do approximate assertions on a complex number type:

```
#[macro_use]
extern crate approx;
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
struct Complex<T> {
    x: T,
    i: T,
}
let x = Complex { x: 1.2, i: 2.3 };
assert_relative_eq!(x, x);
assert_ulps_eq!(x, x, max_ulps = 4);
```
To do this we can implement [ AbsDiffEq](https://docs.rs/trait.AbsDiffEq.html),

[and](https://docs.rs/trait.RelativeEq.html)

`RelativeEq`[generically in terms of a type parameter that also implements](https://docs.rs/trait.UlpsEq.html)

`UlpsEq``AbsDiffEq`, `RelativeEq` and `UlpsEq` respectively.
This means that we can make comparisons for either `Complex<f32>` or `Complex<f64>`:```
impl<T: AbsDiffEq> AbsDiffEq for Complex<T> where
    T::Epsilon: Copy,
{
    type Epsilon = T::Epsilon;
    fn default_epsilon() -> T::Epsilon {
        T::default_epsilon()
    }
    fn abs_diff_eq(&self, other: &Self, epsilon: T::Epsilon) -> bool {
        T::abs_diff_eq(&self.x, &other.x, epsilon) &&
        T::abs_diff_eq(&self.i, &other.i, epsilon)
    }
}
impl<T: RelativeEq> RelativeEq for Complex<T> where
    T::Epsilon: Copy,
{
    fn default_max_relative() -> T::Epsilon {
        T::default_max_relative()
    }
    fn relative_eq(&self, other: &Self, epsilon: T::Epsilon, max_relative: T::Epsilon) -> bool {
        T::relative_eq(&self.x, &other.x, epsilon, max_relative) &&
        T::relative_eq(&self.i, &other.i, epsilon, max_relative)
    }
}
impl<T: UlpsEq> UlpsEq for Complex<T> where
    T::Epsilon: Copy,
{
    fn default_max_ulps() -> u32 {
        T::default_max_ulps()
    }
    fn ulps_eq(&self, other: &Self, epsilon: T::Epsilon, max_ulps: u32) -> bool {
        T::ulps_eq(&self.x, &other.x, epsilon, max_ulps) &&
        T::ulps_eq(&self.i, &other.i, epsilon, max_ulps)
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#references)References

Floating point is hard! Thanks goes to these links for helping to make things a *little*
easier to understand:

# cc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cc/^1/

## Expand description

A library for [Cargo build scripts](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-scripts.html)
to compile a set of C/C++/assembly/CUDA files into a static archive for Cargo
to link into the crate being built. This crate does not compile code itself;
it calls out to the default compiler for the platform. This crate will
automatically detect situations such as cross compilation and
[various environment variables](https://docs.rs#external-configuration-via-environment-variables) and will build code appropriately.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

First, you’ll want to both add a build script for your crate (`build.rs`) and
also add this crate to your `Cargo.toml` via:

```
[build-dependencies]
cc = "1.0"
```
Next up, you’ll want to write a build script like so:

```
// build.rs
cc::Build::new()
    .file("foo.c")
    .file("bar.c")
    .compile("foo");
```
And that’s it! Running `cargo build` should take care of the rest and your Rust
application will now have the C files `foo.c` and `bar.c` compiled into a file
named `libfoo.a`. If the C files contain

`void foo_function(void) { ... }`and

`int32_t bar_function(int32_t x) { ... }`you can call them from Rust by declaring them in your Rust code like so:

```
extern "C" {
    fn foo_function();
    fn bar_function(x: i32) -> i32;
}
pub fn call() {
    unsafe {
        foo_function();
        bar_function(42);
    }
}
fn main() {
    call();
}
```
See [the Rustonomicon](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nomicon/ffi.html) for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#external-configuration-via-environment-variables)External configuration via environment variables

To control the programs and flags used for building, the builder can set a number of different environment variables.

- `CFLAGS`- a series of space separated flags passed to compilers. Note that individual flags cannot currently contain spaces, so doing something like:- `-L=foo\ bar`is not possible.
- `CC`- the actual C compiler used. Note that this supports passing a known wrapper via- `sccache cc`. This compiler must understand the- `-c`flag. For certain- `TARGET`s, it also is assumed to know about other flags (most common is- `-fPIC`). ccache, distcc, sccache, icecc, cachepot and buildcache are supported, for sccache, simply set- `CC`to- `sccache cc`. For other custom- `CC`wrapper, just set- `CC_KNOWN_WRAPPER_CUSTOM`to the custom wrapper used in- `CC`.
- `AR`- the- `ar`(archiver) executable to use to build the static library.
- `CRATE_CC_NO_DEFAULTS`- the default compiler flags may cause conflicts in some cross compiling scenarios. Setting this variable will disable the generation of default compiler flags.
- `CC_ENABLE_DEBUG_OUTPUT`- if set, compiler command invocations and exit codes will be logged to stdout. This is useful for debugging build script issues, but can be overly verbose for normal use.
- `CC_SHELL_ESCAPED_FLAGS`- if set,- `*FLAGS`will be parsed as if they were shell arguments (similar to- `make`and- `cmake`) rather than splitting them on each space. For example, with- `CFLAGS='a "b c"'`, the compiler will be invoked with 2 arguments -- `a`and- `b c`- rather than 3:- `a`,- `"b`and- `c"`.
- `CXX...`- see- [C++ Support](https://docs.rs#c-support).
- `CC_FORCE_DISABLE`- If set,- `cc`will never run any- `Command`- `Error`- `Tool`- `Build::get_compiler`- `cc`runs commands in order to locate compilers. Additionally, this does nothing to prevent users from running- `Tool::to_command`- `Command`
- `RUSTC_WRAPPER`- If set, the specified command will be prefixed to the compiler command. This is useful for projects that want to use- [sccache](https://github.com/mozilla/sccache),- [buildcache](https://gitlab.com/bits-n-bites/buildcache), or- [cachepot](https://github.com/paritytech/cachepot).

Furthermore, projects using this crate may specify custom environment variables
to be inspected, for example via the `Build::try_flags_from_environment`
function. Consult the project’s own documentation or its use of the `cc` crate
for any additional variables it may use.

Each of these variables can also be supplied with certain prefixes and suffixes, in the following prioritized order:

- `<var>_<target>`- for example,- `CC_x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`or- `CC_thumbv8m.main-none-eabi`
- `<var>_<target_with_underscores>`- for example,- `CC_x86_64_unknown_linux_gnu`or- `CC_thumbv8m_main_none_eabi`(both periods and underscores are replaced)
- `<build-kind>_<var>`- for example,- `HOST_CC`or- `TARGET_CFLAGS`
- `<var>`- a plain- `CC`,- `AR`as above.

If none of these variables exist, cc-rs uses built-in defaults.

In addition to the above optional environment variables, `cc-rs` has some
functions with hard requirements on some variables supplied by [cargo’s
build-script driver](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-scripts.html#inputs-to-the-build-script) that it has the `TARGET`, `OUT_DIR`, `OPT_LEVEL`,
and `HOST` variables.

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional features

[§](https://docs.rs#parallel)Parallel

Currently cc-rs supports parallel compilation (think `make -jN`) but this
feature is turned off by default. To enable cc-rs to compile C/C++ in parallel,
you can change your dependency to:

```
[build-dependencies]
cc = { version = "1.0", features = ["parallel"] }
```
By default cc-rs will limit parallelism to `$NUM_JOBS`, or if not present it
will limit it to the number of cpus on the machine. If you are using cargo,
use `-jN` option of `build`, `test` and `run` commands as `$NUM_JOBS`
is supplied by cargo.

[§](https://docs.rs#compile-time-requirements)Compile-time Requirements

To work properly this crate needs access to a C compiler when the build script is being run. This crate does not ship a C compiler with it. The compiler required varies per platform, but there are three broad categories:

- Unix platforms require `cc`to be the C compiler. This can be found by installing cc/clang on Linux distributions and Xcode on macOS, for example.
- Windows platforms targeting MSVC (e.g. your target name ends in `-msvc`) require Visual Studio to be installed.`cc-rs`attempts to locate it, and if it fails,`cl.exe`is expected to be available in`PATH`. This can be set up by running the appropriate developer tools shell.- When using `prefer_clang_cl_over_msvc`, make sure that the`C++ Clang compiler for Windows`component is installed through the Visual Studio Installer, so that`cc-rs`can find`clang-cl.exe`.

- When using
- Windows platforms targeting MinGW (e.g. your target name ends in `-gnu`) require`cc`to be available in`PATH`. We recommend the[MinGW-w64](https://www.mingw-w64.org/)distribution. You may also acquire it via[MSYS2](https://www.msys2.org/), as explained[here](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/master/INSTALL.md#building-on-windows). Make sure to install the appropriate architecture corresponding to your installation of rustc. GCC from older[MinGW](http://www.mingw.org/)project is compatible only with 32-bit rust compiler.

[§](https://docs.rs#c-support)C++ support

`cc-rs` supports C++ libraries compilation by using the `cpp` method on
`Build`:

```
cc::Build::new()
    .cpp(true) // Switch to C++ library compilation.
    .file("foo.cpp")
    .compile("foo");
```
For C++ libraries, the `CXX` and `CXXFLAGS` environment variables are used instead of `CC` and `CFLAGS`.

The C++ standard library may be linked to the crate target. By default it’s `libc++` for macOS, FreeBSD, and OpenBSD, `libc++_shared` for Android, nothing for MSVC, and `libstdc++` for anything else. It can be changed in one of two ways:

- by using the `cpp_link_stdlib`method on`Build`:

```
cc::Build::new()
    .cpp(true)
    .file("foo.cpp")
    .cpp_link_stdlib("stdc++") // use libstdc++
    .compile("foo");
```
- by setting the `CXXSTDLIB`environment variable.

In particular, for Android you may want to [use  c++_static if you have at most one shared library](https://developer.android.com/ndk/guides/cpp-support).

Remember that C++ does name mangling so `extern "C"` might be required to enable Rust linker to find your functions.

[§](https://docs.rs#cuda-c-support)CUDA C++ support

`cc-rs` also supports compiling CUDA C++ libraries by using the `cuda` method
on `Build`:

```
cc::Build::new()
    // Switch to CUDA C++ library compilation using NVCC.
    .cuda(true)
    .cudart("static")
    // Generate code for Maxwell (GTX 970, 980, 980 Ti, Titan X).
    .flag("-gencode").flag("arch=compute_52,code=sm_52")
    // Generate code for Maxwell (Jetson TX1).
    .flag("-gencode").flag("arch=compute_53,code=sm_53")
    // Generate code for Pascal (GTX 1070, 1080, 1080 Ti, Titan Xp).
    .flag("-gencode").flag("arch=compute_61,code=sm_61")
    // Generate code for Pascal (Tesla P100).
    .flag("-gencode").flag("arch=compute_60,code=sm_60")
    // Generate code for Pascal (Jetson TX2).
    .flag("-gencode").flag("arch=compute_62,code=sm_62")
    // Generate code in parallel
    .flag("-t0")
    .file("bar.cu")
    .compile("bar");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#speed-up-compilation-with-sccache)Speed up compilation with sccache

`cc-rs` does not handle incremental compilation like `make` or `ninja`. It
always compiles the all sources, no matter if they have changed or not.
This would be time-consuming in large projects. To save compilation time,
you can use [sccache](https://github.com/mozilla/sccache) by setting
environment variable `RUSTC_WRAPPER=sccache`, which will use cached `.o`
files if the sources are unchanged.

# sidereon_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/sidereon-core/0.11.0/target-redirect/sidereon_core/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#sidereon-core)sidereon-core

The complete Sidereon engine in one crate. It folds the numerical astrodynamics core (orbit propagation, force models, frames, time, SGP4) together with the GNSS domain layer (SP3, broadcast ephemeris, multi-GNSS positioning, RTK/PPP, ionosphere/troposphere, DOP).

- The propagation/astro layer is always present under the `astro`
- The GNSS layer lives behind the default-on `gnss`cargo feature, so a propagation-only consumer can build with`--no-default-features`(plus any astro features it wants) and never compile the IONEX/SP3 parsers.

The GNSS façade is organized by user-facing tasks:

- `ephemeris`
- `rinex`
- `antex`
- `combinations`
- `observables`
- `velocity`
- `positioning`
- `dgnss`
- `quality`
- `observation_qc`
- `signal`
- `ppp_corrections`
- `atmosphere`
- `orbit`

Implementation modules (`sp3`, `rinex_nav`, `spp`, etc.) are crate-private.
This is a clean public surface rather than a compatibility shim around the
original implementation-shaped module layout.

[§](https://docs.rs#units-policy-internal-representation)Units policy (internal representation)

All quantities are stored and computed in **SI base units**, with the frame
and datum encoded in the type name (per the spec’s frames-in-the-type-system
rule), never hidden behind a bare `position_m`:

- **Length / position:**meters (- `_m`). SP3 positions are ITRF/IGS-frame ECEF meters; SPP receiver positions are WGS84/ITRF-compatible ECEF meters. (The- `astro`
- **Time / clock:**seconds (- `_s`). Epochs are represented by the- `astro`- `Instant`/- `TimeScale`), always scale-tagged; there is no bare ambiguous epoch.
- **Velocity:**meters per second (- `_m_s`).
- **Angles:**radians (- `_rad`) internally. Degrees appear only at I/O edges and are named- `_deg`.
- **Frequency:**hertz (- `_hz`).

Field and parameter names carry the unit suffix so the unit is visible at
every call site. Matrix/vector linear algebra uses `nalgebra`
(`DMatrix`/`DVector`) per the spec.

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/sidereon-core/0.11.0/src/sidereon_core/lib.rs.html

# sidereon_core/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! # sidereon-core
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! The complete Sidereon engine in one crate. It folds the numerical
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! astrodynamics core (orbit propagation, force models, frames, time, SGP4)
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! together with the GNSS domain layer (SP3, broadcast ephemeris, multi-GNSS
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! positioning, RTK/PPP, ionosphere/troposphere, DOP).
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//!
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! - The propagation/astro layer is always present under the [`astro`] module.
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! - The GNSS layer lives behind the default-on `gnss` cargo feature, so a
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!   propagation-only consumer can build with `--no-default-features` (plus
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//!   any astro features it wants) and never compile the IONEX/SP3 parsers.
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//!
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! The GNSS façade is organized by user-facing tasks:
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//!
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! - [`ephemeris`] - precise SP3 and broadcast ephemeris products,
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! - [`rinex`] - RINEX navigation/observation parsing and CRINEX decoding,
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! - [`antex`] - ANTEX receiver and satellite antenna calibration parsing,
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! - [`combinations`] - observable linear combinations such as ionosphere-free,
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! - [`observables`] - forward range, Doppler, and azimuth/elevation prediction,
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! - [`velocity`] - receiver velocity and clock-drift solve from range-rate data,
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! - [`positioning`] - single-point positioning and DOP diagnostics,
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! - [`dgnss`] - code-differential pseudorange correction and rover pairing,
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! - [`quality`] - pseudorange weighting, RAIM, and FDE integrity checks,
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! - [`observation_qc`] - RINEX observation completeness and signal rollups,
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! - [`signal`] - GPS C/A code generation, correlation, and acquisition,
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! - [`ppp_corrections`] - static-arc PPP correction precomputation,
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! - [`atmosphere`] - ionosphere and troposphere corrections,
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! - [`orbit`] - compact reduced-orbit fitting/evaluation.
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! Implementation modules (`sp3`, `rinex_nav`, `spp`, etc.) are crate-private.
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! This is a clean public surface rather than a compatibility shim around the
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! original implementation-shaped module layout.
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//!
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! ## Units policy (internal representation)
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//!
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! All quantities are stored and computed in **SI base units**, with the frame
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! and datum encoded in the type name (per the spec's frames-in-the-type-system
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! rule), never hidden behind a bare `position_m`:
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//!
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! - **Length / position:** meters (`_m`). SP3 positions are ITRF/IGS-frame
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//!   ECEF meters; SPP receiver positions are WGS84/ITRF-compatible ECEF meters.
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//!   (The [`astro`] state layer works in kilometers; conversions happen
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!   explicitly at the boundary, never implicitly.)
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! - **Time / clock:** seconds (`_s`). Epochs are represented by the [`astro`]
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//!   time family (`Instant`/`TimeScale`), always scale-tagged; there is no bare
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!   ambiguous epoch.
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! - **Velocity:** meters per second (`_m_s`).
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! - **Angles:** radians (`_rad`) internally. Degrees appear only at I/O edges
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//!   and are named `_deg`.
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! - **Frequency:** hertz (`_hz`).
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//!
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! Field and parameter names carry the unit suffix so the unit is visible at
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! every call site. Matrix/vector linear algebra uses `nalgebra`
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//! (`DMatrix`/`DVector`) per the spec.
[55](https://docs.rs#55)
[56](https://docs.rs#56)extern crate self as sidereon_core;

[60](https://docs.rs#60)// it via `crate::astro::*`.
[61](https://docs.rs#61)// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

[127](https://docs.rs#127)pub mod qc_obs {
[128](https://docs.rs#128)    //! RINEX observation quality-control rollups.

# sidereon_core::astro - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sidereon-core/0.11.0/sidereon_core/astro/index.html

## Expand description

Numerical astrodynamics engine for orbit propagation, force models, and future flight-dynamics primitives.

Current scope:

- inertial Cartesian state representation
- two-body gravity and J2 perturbation
- fixed-step RK4
- adaptive Dormand-Prince 5(4) (`DP54`)
- propagation results with step statistics

Planned future work includes dense output, event handling, richer propagation contexts, additional force models, covariance propagation, estimation, and maneuver support.

# sidereon_core::ephemeris - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sidereon-core/0.11.0/sidereon_core/ephemeris/index.html

## Expand description

Ephemeris products and satellite orbit/clock evaluation.

This is the main public home for loaded GNSS ephemeris data. Use
[ Sp3](https://docs.rs/struct.Sp3.html) for precise SP3 products and

[for broadcast navigation products parsed from RINEX NAV files (or built from records decoded off the air with](https://docs.rs/type.BroadcastEphemeris.html)

`BroadcastEphemeris`[). Both implement](https://docs.rs/struct.BroadcastRecord.html#method.from_lnav)

`BroadcastRecord::from_lnav`[so they can feed](https://docs.rs/trait.EphemerisSource.html)

`EphemerisSource`[; the broadcast-only real-time/offline path is](https://docs.rs/positioning/fn.solve.html)

`crate::positioning::solve`[and the precise-with-broadcast-fallback path is](https://docs.rs/positioning/fn.solve_broadcast.html)

`solve_broadcast`[.](https://docs.rs/positioning/fn.solve_with_fallback.html)

`solve_with_fallback`## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

# sidereon_core::combinations - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sidereon-core/0.11.0/sidereon_core/combinations/index.html

## Expand description

GNSS observable linear combinations.

The ionosphere-free code and carrier-phase combinations are pure
frequency-domain algebra. The operation order is intentionally simple and
pinned to the original Sidereon/SciPy oracle recipe: square each carrier first,
form `gamma = f1^2 / (f1^2 - f2^2)`, then evaluate
`gamma * obs1 - (gamma - 1) * obs2` with normal Rust arithmetic.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use crate::frequencies::`- [CarrierBand](https://docs.rs/frequencies/enum.CarrierBand.html);
- `pub use crate::frequencies::`- [CarrierFrequency](https://docs.rs/frequencies/struct.CarrierFrequency.html);
- `pub use crate::frequencies::`- [CarrierPair](https://docs.rs/frequencies/struct.CarrierPair.html);

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Ionosphere](https://docs.rs/enum.IonosphereFreeError.html)- Free - Error
- Error produced by ionosphere-free combination helpers.
- [Pseudorange](https://docs.rs/enum.PseudorangeDropReason.html)- Drop - Reason
- Reason a satellite was not included in a paired pseudorange result.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [carrier_](https://docs.rs/fn.carrier_frequencies.html)- frequencies
- The full carrier-frequency table for the supported standard pairs.
- [carrier_](https://docs.rs/fn.carrier_frequency_hz.html)- frequency_ - hz
- The standard carrier frequency in hertz for a constellation and band.
- [default_](https://docs.rs/fn.default_pair.html)- pair
- Standard dual-frequency ionosphere-free carrier pair for a constellation.

# sidereon_core::velocity - Rust

## Expand description

Receiver velocity and clock-drift solve from GNSS range-rate observations.

The caller supplies a known receiver position plus one epoch of pseudorange-rate or Doppler observations; the core builds the deterministic normal equations and returns receiver velocity, clock drift, residuals, and used-satellite ordering.

# sidereon_core::signal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sidereon-core/0.11.0/sidereon_core/signal/index.html

## Expand description

GPS L1 C/A code generation, coherent correlation, and acquisition.

The functions here are deterministic time-domain signal primitives. They intentionally keep the same simple operation order as the original Sidereon implementation: C/A chips are generated by clocking the two IS-GPS-200 LFSRs, sampled by zero-order hold, and correlation/acquisition are direct nested sums over samples and Doppler bins.

# sidereon_core::orbit - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sidereon-core/0.11.0/sidereon_core/orbit/index.html

## Expand description

Compact orbit approximations.

Reduced orbits are fitted approximations for caching, transport, and quick
visibility math. They are not precise ephemeris products; use
[ crate::ephemeris::Sp3](https://docs.rs/ephemeris/struct.Sp3.html) or

[when full-fidelity products are available.](https://docs.rs/ephemeris/type.BroadcastEphemeris.html)

`crate::ephemeris::BroadcastEphemeris`## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Calendar](https://docs.rs/struct.CalendarEpoch.html)- Epoch
- A UTC calendar instant `(year, month, day, hour, minute, second)`, the form the core`TimeScales::from_utc``Instant`->`TimeScales`bridge exists in the core crate, so the calendar tuple is carried explicitly to the boundary.
- [Drift](https://docs.rs/struct.DriftEntry.html)- Entry
- A per-epoch drift entry: the model-vs-truth position error at one epoch.
- [Drift](https://docs.rs/struct.DriftReport.html)- Report
- The result of a source-backed drift evaluation.
- [Ecef](https://docs.rs/struct.EcefSample.html)- Sample
- One fitting/drift truth sample: an epoch and an ECEF (ITRF) position in meters.
- [Elements](https://docs.rs/struct.Elements.html)
- The fitted mean elements plus the kept J2 seed.
- [FitStats](https://docs.rs/struct.FitStats.html)
- Residual statistics from a fit, in meters.
- [Piecewise](https://docs.rs/struct.PiecewiseOrbit.html)- Orbit
- A long span represented by contiguous independently-fitted reduced-orbit segments.
- [Piecewise](https://docs.rs/struct.PiecewiseOrbitSourceFit.html)- Orbit - Source - Fit
- A source-backed piecewise fit and its sampling metadata.
- [Piecewise](https://docs.rs/struct.PiecewiseOrbitSourceFitOptions.html)- Orbit - Source - FitOptions
- Options for `fit_piecewise_reduced_orbit_source`
- [Piecewise](https://docs.rs/struct.PiecewiseSegment.html)- Segment
- One fitted segment in a piecewise reduced-orbit model.
- [Reduced](https://docs.rs/struct.ReducedOrbit.html)- Orbit
- A fitted model: elements plus the residual statistics of the fit.
- [Reduced](https://docs.rs/struct.ReducedOrbitSourceDrift.html)- Orbit - Source - Drift
- A source-backed single-model drift report and its sampling metadata.
- [Reduced](https://docs.rs/struct.ReducedOrbitSourceDriftOptions.html)- Orbit - Source - Drift - Options
- Options for `drift_reduced_orbit_source`
- [Reduced](https://docs.rs/struct.ReducedOrbitSourceFit.html)- Orbit - Source - Fit
- A source-backed single-model fit and its sampling metadata.
- [Reduced](https://docs.rs/struct.ReducedOrbitSourceFitOptions.html)- Orbit - Source - FitOptions
- Options for `fit_reduced_orbit_source`
- [Reduced](https://docs.rs/struct.ReducedOrbitSourceSampling.html)- Orbit - Source - Sampling
- Sampling window and cadence for source-backed reduced-orbit drivers.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Frame](https://docs.rs/enum.Frame.html)
- Which reference frame a position/velocity result is expressed in.
- [Model](https://docs.rs/enum.Model.html)
- Which mean-element model the fit and evaluation use.
- [Piecewise](https://docs.rs/enum.PiecewiseOrbitError.html)- Orbit - Error
- Errors from fitting or evaluating a piecewise reduced orbit.
- [Reduced](https://docs.rs/enum.ReducedOrbitError.html)- Orbit - Error
- Errors from fitting or evaluating a reduced orbit.
- [Reduced](https://docs.rs/enum.ReducedOrbitSource.html)- Orbit - Source
- Source used by source-backed reduced-orbit fit and drift drivers.
- [Reduced](https://docs.rs/enum.ReducedOrbitSourceError.html)- Orbit - Source - Error
- Error returned by source-backed reduced-orbit drivers.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [MIN_](https://docs.rs/constant.MIN_SAMPLES.html)- SAMPLES
- Minimum number of samples the fitter accepts. The circular model solves five free elements and the eccentric model eight; each ECEF sample contributes three residuals, so four well-spread samples (twelve residuals) is the floor. Below this the geometry seed and refinement are unreliable.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [drift](https://docs.rs/fn.drift.html)
- Evaluate the model against truth ECEF samples and report the per-epoch error,
its statistics, and the first epoch the error crosses `threshold_m`.
- [drift_](https://docs.rs/fn.drift_piecewise_reduced_orbit_source.html)- piecewise_ - reduced_ - orbit_ - source
- Sample an SP3 or SGP4 source and evaluate a piecewise model’s drift.
- [drift_](https://docs.rs/fn.drift_reduced_orbit_source.html)- reduced_ - orbit_ - source
- Sample an SP3 or SGP4 source and evaluate drift against those truth samples.
- [fit](https://docs.rs/fn.fit.html)
- Fit the default `circular_secular`model to ECEF samples, with all epochs interpreted in`scale`(e.g. an SP3 product’s GPST).
- [fit_](https://docs.rs/fn.fit_piecewise.html)- piecewise
- Fit contiguous reduced-orbit segments over `[t0, t1]`.
- [fit_](https://docs.rs/fn.fit_piecewise_reduced_orbit_source.html)- piecewise_ - reduced_ - orbit_ - source
- Sample an SP3 or SGP4 source and fit a piecewise reduced orbit.
- [fit_](https://docs.rs/fn.fit_reduced_orbit_source.html)- reduced_ - orbit_ - source
- Sample an SP3 or SGP4 source and fit a reduced orbit.
- [fit_](https://docs.rs/fn.fit_with_model.html)- with_ - model
- Fit a chosen `Model``scale`.
- [piecewise_](https://docs.rs/fn.piecewise_drift.html)- drift
- Evaluate a piecewise model against truth ECEF samples.
- [piecewise_](https://docs.rs/fn.piecewise_position.html)- position
- Evaluate a piecewise reduced orbit at `epoch`.
- [piecewise_](https://docs.rs/fn.piecewise_position_velocity.html)- position_ - velocity
- Evaluate piecewise reduced-orbit position and velocity at `epoch`.
- [position](https://docs.rs/fn.position.html)
- Evaluate the model position at `epoch`(interpreted in`scale`) in the requested frame, meters.
- [position_](https://docs.rs/fn.position_velocity.html)- velocity
- Evaluate the model position and velocity at `epoch`in the requested frame. Returns`(position_m, velocity_m_s)`. ECEF velocity includes the Earth-rotation transport term.
- [select_](https://docs.rs/fn.select_piecewise_segment.html)- piecewise_ - segment
- Return the segment covering `epoch`.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/type.Error.html)
- Error type returned by reduced-orbit fitting/evaluation.
- [Reduced](https://docs.rs/type.ReducedOrbitModel.html)- Orbit - Model
- Role-oriented alias for a fitted reduced-orbit model.

# geodetic_to_itrf in sidereon_core::frame - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sidereon-core/0.11.0/sidereon_core/frame/fn.geodetic_to_itrf.html

```
pub fn geodetic_to_itrf(
    geodetic:
```
[Wgs84Geodetic](https://docs.rs/struct.Wgs84Geodetic.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[ItrfPositionM](https://docs.rs/struct.ItrfPositionM.html), [FrameTransformError](https://docs.rs/astro/frames/transforms/enum.FrameTransformError.html)>## Expand description

Convert a WGS84 geodetic position to an ITRF/ECEF position.

Free-function wrapper over the crate’s single validated forward converter
[ crate::astro::frames::transforms::geodetic_to_itrs](https://docs.rs/astro/frames/transforms/fn.geodetic_to_itrs.html) (the same WGS84 math
the positioning paths use); this only bridges the typed frame values and
their units (the frame types carry radians + meters, the internal converter
works in degrees + kilometers). No conversion math is reimplemented here.

# ItrfPositionM in sidereon_core::frame - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sidereon-core/0.11.0/sidereon_core/frame/struct.ItrfPositionM.html

## Expand description

A position in the ITRF / IGS-realization Earth-Centered-Earth-Fixed frame,
expressed in **meters**.

SP3 ephemerides are published in an IGS realization of the ITRF (e.g.
`IGS14`, `IGS20`); the exact realization string is carried on the SP3
header ([ crate::sp3::Sp3Header::coordinate_system](https://docs.rs/ephemeris/struct.Sp3Header.html#structfield.coordinate_system)), while this type fixes
the

*kind*of frame (ITRF/IGS ECEF) and the

*unit*(meters) in the type system. There is intentionally no implicit conversion to the core crate’s kilometer states; conversion happens explicitly at an API boundary.

# Wgs84Geodetic in sidereon_core::frame - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sidereon-core/0.11.0/sidereon_core/frame/struct.Wgs84Geodetic.html

## Expand description

A geodetic (ellipsoidal) position on the WGS84 datum.

Latitude and longitude are geodetic angles in **radians**; height is the
ellipsoidal height in **meters**. This is the receiver-position type the
atmospheric (ionosphere/troposphere) models take: they need the geodetic
latitude/longitude of the antenna and, for the troposphere, the height.

The frame and units are fixed in the type so a caller cannot mix this with
the ECEF [ ItrfPositionM](https://docs.rs/struct.ItrfPositionM.html) or pass degrees where radians are expected.
Longitude is positive east; latitude is positive north.

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.lat_rad)

`lat_rad: `[f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html)Geodetic latitude in radians, positive north, range `[-pi/2, pi/2]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.lon_rad)

`lon_rad: `[f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html)Geodetic longitude in radians, positive east, range `[-pi, pi]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.height_m)

`height_m: `[f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html)Ellipsoidal height above the WGS84 ellipsoid in meters.

# ellipsoidal_height_m in sidereon_core::geoid - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sidereon-core/0.11.0/sidereon_core/geoid/fn.ellipsoidal_height_m.html

## Expand description

Ellipsoidal height `h = H + N` (metres above the WGS84 ellipsoid) from an
orthometric height and a geodetic position in radians, using the COARSE
30-degree built-in model’s undulation (decametre-level error, NOT
survey-grade). For metre-class conversion use [ egm96_ellipsoidal_height_m](https://docs.rs/fn.egm96_ellipsoidal_height_m.html);
for a real model, add

[directly.](https://docs.rs/struct.GeoidGrid.html#method.undulation_rad)

`GeoidGrid::undulation_rad`

---

# geoid_undulation in sidereon_core::geoid - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sidereon-core/0.11.0/sidereon_core/geoid/fn.geoid_undulation.html

## Expand description

Geoid undulation `N` (metres above the WGS84 ellipsoid) at a geodetic
position in radians, from the COARSE built-in global grid.

Latitude is positive north, longitude positive east, both in radians. See
the module docs for the built-in-grid-vs-real-model trade-off: for accuracy
load a real model with [ GeoidGrid::from_text](https://docs.rs/struct.GeoidGrid.html#method.from_text) and call

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.GeoidGrid.html#method.undulation_rad)

`GeoidGrid::undulation_rad`

A grid spacing or origin was non-finite or non-positive.

A grid sample value was non-finite.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Parse)

### Parse

The grid text could not be parsed.

# sidereon_core::carrier_phase - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sidereon-core/0.11.0/sidereon_core/carrier_phase/index.html

## Expand description

Carrier-phase combinations, cycle-slip detection, and Hatch smoothing.

This module owns the language-independent modeling behind Sidereon’
`CarrierPhase` API: phase-cycle conversion, geometry-free and
Melbourne-Wubbena combinations, loss-of-lock/GF/MW/data-gap cycle-slip
classification, and single/dual-frequency Hatch smoothing.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use crate::tolerances::`- [FREQUENCY_DENOMINATOR_EPS_HZ](https://docs.rs/tolerances/constant.FREQUENCY_DENOMINATOR_EPS_HZ.html)as FREQ_EPSILON_HZ;

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [ArcEpoch](https://docs.rs/struct.ArcEpoch.html)
- One epoch in a single-satellite carrier-phase arc.
- [Cycle](https://docs.rs/struct.CycleSlipOptions.html)- Slip - Options
- Options controlling cycle-slip classification.
- [Iono](https://docs.rs/struct.IonoFreeSmoothResult.html)- Free - Smooth - Result
- Hatch-smoothed ionosphere-free code output for one epoch.
- [Slip](https://docs.rs/struct.SlipResult.html)- Result
- Cycle-slip classification for one input epoch.
- [Smooth](https://docs.rs/struct.SmoothCodeResult.html)- Code - Result
- Hatch-smoothed single-frequency code output for one epoch.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Carrier](https://docs.rs/enum.CarrierPhaseError.html)- Phase - Error
- Error produced by carrier-phase scalar combinations.
- [Slip](https://docs.rs/enum.SlipReason.html)- Reason

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_GF_THRESHOLD_M.html)- GF_ - THRESHOLD_ - M
- Default geometry-free cycle-slip threshold, meters.
- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_HATCH_WINDOW_CAP.html)- HATCH_ - WINDOW_ - CAP
- Default Hatch carrier-smoothing window cap, in epochs.
- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_MIN_ARC_GAP_S.html)- MIN_ - ARC_ - GAP_ - S
- Default maximum gap between consecutive usable arc samples, seconds.
- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_MW_THRESHOLD_CYCLES.html)- MW_ - THRESHOLD_ - CYCLES

- Code-minus-carrier diagnostic `CMC = P - L`, meters.
- [detect_](https://docs.rs/fn.detect_cycle_slips.html)- cycle_ - slips
- Detect cycle slips on a time-ordered single-satellite arc.

- Geometry-free phase combination `L_GF = L1 - L2`, meters.
- [melbourne_](https://docs.rs/fn.melbourne_wubbena.html)- wubbena

- [narrow_](https://docs.rs/fn.narrow_lane_code.html)- lane_ - code

- [phase_](https://docs.rs/fn.phase_meters.html)- meters
- Carrier phase in meters, `L = c / f * phi`.
- [smooth_](https://docs.rs/fn.smooth_code.html)- code

- Dual-frequency ionosphere-free Hatch carrier-smoothed code.
- [wide_](https://docs.rs/fn.wide_lane_cycles.html)- lane_ - cycles

`(MW combination) / lambda_WL`.
- [wide_](https://docs.rs/fn.wide_lane_wavelength.html)- lane_ - wavelength
- Wide-lane wavelength `lambda_WL = c / (f1 - f2)`, meters.

# sidereon_core::constellation - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sidereon-core/0.11.0/sidereon_core/constellation/index.html

## Expand description

GNSS constellation identity catalog and validation helpers.

This is a data/catalog layer: it builds normalized satellite identity records from public sources and compares those records with GNSS products. It does not alter positioning solves or infer application-specific health rules. It is deterministic and performs no network access; fetching the source bytes is the caller’s (binding’s) job.

GPS, Galileo, GLONASS, BeiDou, and QZSS are supported. The base source for
every system is a CelesTrak OMM/JSON group (`gps-ops`, `galileo`, `glo-ops`,
`beidou`, and the QZSS members of the `gnss` group); the within-system PRN /
slot is parsed from `OBJECT_NAME` and rendered as the SP3/RINEX id (`"G13"`,
`"E07"`, `"R13"`, `"C19"`, `"J02"`) via [ gnss_sp3_id](https://docs.rs/fn.gnss_sp3_id.html). Each constellation
names its satellites differently, so

[dispatches on](https://docs.rs/fn.from_celestrak_omm.html)

`from_celestrak_omm`[to a per-system identity adapter:](https://docs.rs/enum.GnssSystem.html)

`GnssSystem`- **GPS:**- `(PRN nn)`in the object name is the PRN directly.
- **BeiDou:**- `(Cnn)`in the object name is the PRN directly.
- **QZSS:**- `(QZSS/PRN nnn)`carries the broadcast PRN (193..=201); the RINEX slot is- `nnn - 192`(- `J01`..- `J09`), per RINEX 3.0x.
- **Galileo:**the object name is the- `GSATdddd`build id, which carries no PRN; the SVID/PRN is resolved from the published GSAT->SVID table- `galileo_prn_for_gsat`
- **GLONASS:**the parenthesized number is the GLONASS (Uragan) number, not the orbital slot; the slot is resolved from the published slot table- `glonass_slot_for_number`- `glonass_fdma_channel`

NAVCEN’s GPS constellation status page can be parsed and merged as an optional overlay for SVN and NANU usability details. There is no clean equivalent health oracle for the other systems, so usability overlays are GPS-only; the OMM identity round-trip and the GLONASS FDMA check are the gates for the rest.

The OMM input is the canonical [ Omm](https://docs.rs/astro/omm/struct.Omm.html) produced by
the core OMM parser (

`crate::astro::omm::{parse_json, parse_json_array}`):
this module does not re-parse OMM from scratch, it reads `OBJECT_NAME` and
`NORAD_CAT_ID` off already-parsed records.```
use sidereon_core::constellation::{to_csv, BoolStyle, Record, RecordSource};
use sidereon_core::GnssSystem;
let record = Record {
    system: GnssSystem::Gps,
    prn: 3,
    svn: None,
    norad_id: 40294,
    sp3_id: "G03".to_string(),
    fdma_channel: None,
    active: true,
    usable: true,
    source: RecordSource::default(),
};
assert_eq!(
    to_csv(&[record], BoolStyle::Lower),
    "prn,norad_cat_id,active,sp3_id\n3,40294,true,G03\n"
);
```

# sidereon_core::estimation - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sidereon-core/0.11.0/sidereon_core/estimation/index.html

## Expand description

GNSS estimation substrate (Phase-2).

The Phase-2 redesign collapses the three thick estimator stacks
(`spp`, `rtk`/`rtk_filter`, `precise_positioning`) onto one shared estimation
substrate plus thin, runtime-selectable strategies. The mechanism that keeps
every external reference bit-exact through the migration is the NAMED recipe:
a strategy selects the floating-point operation order it needs by enum value,
never by owning a private copy of a parity-sensitive helper.

P0 landed [ recipe](https://docs.rs/recipe/index.html) - the taxonomy of operation-order variants, each
documented against the current code path it names and defaulting to current
behavior. P1 adds [

`substrate`] with the frame and range kernels; P2 adds the
parameter layout, the weighted measurement row, the measurement covariance
block, and the normal-equation assembler; P3 adds the shared ambiguity and qc
kernels, all routed through by the existing strategies via their current
recipe. P4 adds [: the runtime](https://docs.rs/strategies/index.html)

`strategies`[selector (](https://docs.rs/recipe/enum.StrategyId.html)

`StrategyId`[) that resolves a strategy into its recipe and screen/ambiguity policy data and dispatches to the technique’s reference entry point, leaving every existing 0-ULP golden unchanged.](https://docs.rs/strategies/fn.estimate.html)

`strategies::estimate`## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use recipe::`- [AmbiguityIdPolicy](https://docs.rs/recipe/struct.AmbiguityIdPolicy.html);

# sidereon_core::frame - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sidereon-core/0.11.0/sidereon_core/frame/index.html

## Expand description

Frame-tagged position types.

Every position value encodes its reference frame and datum in the **type
name**, never a bare `position_m` that hides the frame. SP3 products give
satellite states
in the ITRF/IGS-realization ECEF frame, in meters; that fact is carried by
[ ItrfPositionM](https://docs.rs/struct.ItrfPositionM.html) so a consumer cannot accidentally mix it with, say, a
GCRS/TEME state from the core crate (which is in kilometers).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Itrf](https://docs.rs/struct.ItrfPositionM.html)- PositionM
- A position in the ITRF / IGS-realization Earth-Centered-Earth-Fixed frame,
expressed in **meters**.
- [Itrf](https://docs.rs/struct.ItrfVelocityMS.html)- VelocityMS
- A velocity in the ITRF / IGS-realization ECEF frame, in **meters per second**.
- [Wgs84](https://docs.rs/struct.Wgs84Geodetic.html)- Geodetic
- A geodetic (ellipsoidal) position on the WGS84 datum.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Frame](https://docs.rs/enum.FrameValueError.html)- Value - Error
- Error returned when constructing frame-tagged values from invalid inputs.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [geocentric_](https://docs.rs/fn.geocentric_east.html)- east
- East unit of the geocentric local frame for a given local `up`:`normalize(Z x up)`, degenerating to`+X`when`up`is parallel to`Z`.
- [geocentric_](https://docs.rs/fn.geocentric_neu_basis.html)- neu_ - basis
- Geocentric local North-East-Up basis at a receiver ECEF position, returned as
`(north, east, up)`.
- [geocentric_](https://docs.rs/fn.geocentric_up.html)- up
- Geocentric local vertical at a receiver ECEF position: the position vector normalized (the spherical radial direction, out from the geocenter).
- [geodetic_](https://docs.rs/fn.geodetic_to_itrf.html)- to_ - itrf

# sidereon_core::geoid - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sidereon-core/0.11.0/sidereon_core/geoid/index.html

## Expand description

Geoid undulation (geoid height) lookup with bilinear interpolation.

The geoid undulation `N` is the height of the geoid (mean sea level
equipotential surface) above the WGS84 reference ellipsoid, in metres.
GNSS positioning yields the ellipsoidal height `h`; the orthometric height
`H` (height above mean sea level) is

`H = h - N`A geoid model is published as a regular latitude/longitude grid of `N`
samples (EGM96, EGM2008, and the national models all ship this way). This
module provides:

- `GeoidGrid`- `GeoidGrid::undulation_rad`- `GeoidGrid::undulation_deg`
- `GeoidGrid::from_text`
- `GeoidGrid::from_egm96_dac`- `WW15MGH.DAC`) for decimetre-class datum work;
- `egm96_undulation`- `egm96_grid`
- `geoid_undulation`- `orthometric_height_m`- `ellipsoidal_height_m`

[§](https://docs.rs#choosing-a-grid)Choosing a grid

Three accuracy tiers are available, in increasing fidelity:

- `geoid_undulation`
- `egm96_undulation`
- `GeoidGrid::from_egm96_dac`- `WW15MGH.DAC`file (a ~2 MB download, not vendored here) - the full 15-arcminute resolution. Its bilinear lookup tracks the geoid to roughly decimetre RMS, but the worst-case bilinear interpolation error can still exceed 1 m over the steepest geoid gradients (see- [https://geographiclib.sourceforge.io/html/geoid.html](https://geographiclib.sourceforge.io/html/geoid.html)for the egm96-15 error envelope), so this path supports decimetre-class typical datum work rather than guaranteed sub-metre accuracy everywhere. Embedding the full grid is impractical (the 15-arcminute grid is ~1 M samples and EGM2008 1-minute is ~2.3 GB), so the high-resolution path loads the file at runtime.

A caller with any other vendor grid can lower it to [ GeoidGrid::from_text](https://docs.rs/struct.GeoidGrid.html#method.from_text)
or build a

[via](https://docs.rs/struct.GeoidGrid.html)

`GeoidGrid`[and call](https://docs.rs/struct.GeoidGrid.html#method.new)

`GeoidGrid::new`[directly.](https://docs.rs/struct.GeoidGrid.html#method.undulation_rad)

`GeoidGrid::undulation_rad`## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Geoid](https://docs.rs/struct.GeoidGrid.html)- Grid
- A regular latitude/longitude grid of geoid undulation samples (metres) with bilinear interpolation.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Geoid](https://docs.rs/enum.GeoidError.html)- Error
- Why a geoid grid could not be constructed or parsed.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [egm96_](https://docs.rs/fn.egm96_ellipsoidal_height_m.html)- ellipsoidal_ - height_ - m
- Ellipsoidal height `h = H + N`(metres above the WGS84 ellipsoid) from an orthometric height and a geodetic position in radians, using the embedded GENUINE EGM96 1-degree model via`egm96_undulation`
- [egm96_](https://docs.rs/fn.egm96_grid.html)- grid
- The embedded genuine EGM96 1-degree global geoid, decoded once on first use.
- [egm96_](https://docs.rs/fn.egm96_orthometric_height_m.html)- orthometric_ - height_ - m
- Orthometric height `H = h - N`(metres above mean sea level) from an ellipsoidal height and a geodetic position in radians, using the embedded GENUINE EGM96 1-degree model via`egm96_undulation`
- [egm96_](https://docs.rs/fn.egm96_undulation.html)- undulation
- Geoid undulation `N`(metres above the WGS84 ellipsoid) at a geodetic position in radians, from the embedded GENUINE EGM96 1-degree global grid.

# sidereon_core::ils - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sidereon-core/0.11.0/sidereon_core/ils/index.html

## Expand description

Integer least squares - ambiguity-resolution kernels for precise / RTK positioning.

The bounded kernel preserves the historical public score/order contract:
Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting (max-abs pivot, first-index tie
break, `<= PIVOT_EPSILON` singular guard), `Δᵀ Q⁻¹ Δ` summation order (i-outer,
j-inner, left-associated products), lattice enumeration, and `{score, cycles}`
candidate ordering. The LAMBDA kernel is a faithful RTKLIB `lambda()` port.
Crate-side tests pin the RTKLIB oracle fixture plus frozen output bits. All
arithmetic is plain `*` / `-` / `+` (no FMA), per the crate’s reproducibility
rule.

These kernels live in Rust because the bounded search, LAMBDA, and the partial-ambiguity subset search built on top of them are compute hot paths for multi-epoch RTK arcs.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [IlsResult](https://docs.rs/struct.IlsResult.html)
- Outcome of a bounded ILS search.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [IlsError](https://docs.rs/enum.IlsError.html)
- Why a bounded ILS search could not produce a result. Mapped by the NIF onto
the reference Elixir error tuples (`:singular_geometry`,`{:no_integer_candidates, n}`,`{:too_many_integer_candidates, n, limit}`).

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [bounded_](https://docs.rs/fn.bounded_ils_search.html)- ils_ - search
- Bounded integer least squares over the lattice within `radius`integers of each rounded float ambiguity.
- [lambda_](https://docs.rs/fn.lambda_ils_search.html)- ils_ - search
- Correct integer-least-squares via the LAMBDA method (RTKLIB `lambda()`port).

# sidereon_core::rtcm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sidereon-core/0.11.0/sidereon_core/rtcm/index.html

## Expand description

RTCM 3 differential-GNSS stream decoding and encoding.

RTCM 10403.x (“RTCM Standard for Differential GNSS Services, Version 3”) is the dominant wire format for real-time GNSS correction and observation streams: base-station observations, reference coordinates, antenna metadata, and broadcast ephemerides flow from a caster to a rover as a sequence of framed binary messages. This module is a sans-I/O codec for that stream, built to the same shape as the crate’s RINEX / SP3 / IONEX parsers:

- a forgiving byte-level frame layer ([`framing`]) that syncs on the`0xD3`preamble, reads the 10-bit length, and verifies the 24-bit CRC-24Q;
- a format-agnostic canonical IR (`Message`
- an encoder that turns the IR back into bytes, so a decode followed by an encode round-trips byte-for-byte.

[§](https://docs.rs#message-coverage)Message coverage

Decoded and encoded:

| Message | Numbers | IR type |
|---|---|---|
| MSM4 observations | 1074 / 1084 / 1094 / 1104 / 1114 / 1124 / 1134 | `MsmMessage` |
| MSM7 observations | 1077 / 1087 / 1097 / 1107 / 1117 / 1127 / 1137 | `MsmMessage` |
| Station coordinates | 1005 / 1006 | `StationCoordinates` |
| Antenna / receiver | 1007 / 1008 / 1033 | `AntennaDescriptor` |
| GPS ephemeris | 1019 | `GpsEphemeris` |
| GLONASS ephemeris | 1020 | `GlonassEphemeris` |

Any other message number is preserved losslessly as [ Message::Unsupported](https://docs.rs/enum.Message.html#variant.Unsupported)
(its raw body is kept so the frame still round-trips). Deferred message types
include the other MSM variants (MSM1/2/3/5/6), the legacy L1/L1-L2
observation messages (1001-1004, 1009-1012), the network-RTK and SSR
correction families, and the Galileo / BeiDou / QZSS ephemerides
(1042-1046). They decode as

`Unsupported` rather than erroring.[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick start

```
use sidereon_core::rtcm::{self, Message, StationCoordinates};
// Build a 1006 reference-coordinate message and frame it.
let station = StationCoordinates {
    message_number: 1006,
    reference_station_id: 2003,
    itrf_realization_year: 0,
    gps_indicator: true,
    glonass_indicator: true,
    galileo_indicator: false,
    reference_station_indicator: false,
    ecef_x: 11_446_021_400,
    single_receiver_oscillator: false,
    reserved: false,
    ecef_y: -7_415_136_500,
    quarter_cycle_indicator: 0,
    ecef_z: 12_602_528_900,
    antenna_height: Some(15_000),
};
// A constructed message encodes either directly on the typed value or
// through the [`Message`] wrapper; both produce the same body bytes.
let body = station.encode();
assert_eq!(body, Message::StationCoordinates(station).encode());
let frame = rtcm::encode_frame(&body).unwrap();
// Decode it back out of the framed stream.
let decoded = rtcm::decode_messages(&frame);
assert_eq!(decoded.len(), 1);
match &decoded[0] {
    Message::StationCoordinates(s) => assert_eq!(s.reference_station_id, 2003),
    _ => panic!("expected station coordinates"),
}
```

- RINEX LLI bit 1: half-cycle ambiguity or half-cycle slip is possible.
- [LLI_](https://docs.rs/constant.LLI_LOSS_OF_LOCK.html)- LOSS_ - OF_ - LOCK
- RINEX LLI bit 0: loss of lock, so a cycle slip is possible.

- The RTCM 3 frame preamble byte.

# sidereon_core::rtk - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sidereon-core/0.11.0/sidereon_core/rtk/index.html

RTK double-difference primitives.

This module owns the language-independent carrier/code double-difference construction used by Sidereon’ public RTK API.

# sidereon_core::ssr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sidereon-core/0.11.0/sidereon_core/ssr/index.html

## Expand description

Engineering-unit State Space Representation corrections.

The RTCM module stores raw transmitted integers. This module stores scaled correction values keyed by satellite, with enough provider and issue metadata to apply orbit and clock corrections on top of broadcast ephemerides.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- Clock correction for one satellite.
- [SsrCode](https://docs.rs/struct.SsrCodeBias.html)- Bias

- [SsrCorrected](https://docs.rs/struct.SsrCorrectedEphemeris.html)- Ephemeris
- Broadcast ephemeris corrected by an SSR store.
- [SsrCorrected](https://docs.rs/struct.SsrCorrectedEphemerisOwned.html)- Ephemeris - Owned
- Owned corrected ephemeris source.
- [SsrCorrection](https://docs.rs/struct.SsrCorrectionStore.html)- Store
- Active SSR corrections keyed by satellite.
- [SsrFallback](https://docs.rs/struct.SsrFallbackPolicy.html)- Policy
- Missing-correction and regional policy for corrected ephemerides.
- [SsrHigh](https://docs.rs/struct.SsrHighRateClock.html)- Rate - Clock
- High-rate clock correction for one satellite.
- [SsrOrbit](https://docs.rs/struct.SsrOrbitCorrection.html)- Correction

# sidereon_core::staleness - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sidereon-core/0.11.0/sidereon_core/staleness/index.html

## Expand description

Product-staleness graceful degradation for time-varying GNSS products.

Time-varying products (IONEX TEC maps, rapid/predicted SP3 orbit/clock files) publish with latency and gaps, so the product for the exact requested epoch is not always on hand. A direct lookup against a missing epoch is a hard failure, which is brittle for real-time and operational use.

This module sits on top of the [ Ionex](https://docs.rs/atmosphere/ionosphere/struct.Ionex.html) and

[parsers and adds a selection layer that degrades gracefully instead of erroring: given a SET of available parsed products and a requested epoch (or epoch range), it returns a usable handle, falling back to the most-recent available product within a configurable staleness cap. Every result carries](https://docs.rs/ephemeris/struct.Sp3.html)

`Sp3`[describing which source epoch was used, how stale it is, and the](https://docs.rs/struct.StalenessMetadata.html)

`StalenessMetadata`[, so a degraded answer is never substituted silently. Only a request that exceeds the staleness cap fails, with a typed](https://docs.rs/enum.DegradationKind.html)

`DegradationKind`[.](https://docs.rs/enum.SelectionError.html)

`SelectionError`[§](https://docs.rs#degradation-paths)Degradation paths

- **Exact**: a product covering the requested epoch is present. The original product is returned untouched and the downstream evaluation is bit-for-bit identical to calling the parser/interpolator directly. Staleness is zero.
- **IONEX diurnal shift**: when no product covers the requested day, the most-recent prior day’s grid is advanced by whole days onto the requested epoch (- `Ionex::with_map_epochs_shifted_days`
- **SP3 nearest-prior**: when no product covers the requested epoch, the most-recent prior product is selected as-is, with the staleness measured from its last epoch.

[§](https://docs.rs#network)Network

This layer is pure and no-network: it selects among products the caller has already parsed. Fetching the products is a per-binding concern.

# sidereon_core::tides - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sidereon-core/0.11.0/sidereon_core/tides/index.html

## Expand description

Solid-earth tide station displacement (IERS Conventions, Chapter 7).

[ solid_earth_tide](https://docs.rs/fn.solid_earth_tide.html) computes the tidal displacement of an Earth-fixed (ITRF)
GNSS station caused by the lunar and solar gravitational attraction. It is a
derived work of the IERS Conventions (2010) reference routine

`DEHANTTIDEINEL.F` (and its companion routines `ST1IDIU`, `ST1ISEM`,
`ST1L1`, `STEP2DIU`, `STEP2LON`, `CAL2JD`, `DAT`), reproduced here in Rust.How this derived work is based upon and differs from the original Software:

- It is a line-for-line Rust translation of the in-phase degree-2/degree-3
displacement, the out-of-phase corrections (`ST1IDIU`,`ST1ISEM`), the latitude-dependence correction (`ST1L1`), and the frequency-dependent step-2 diurnal/long-period band corrections (`STEP2DIU`,`STEP2LON`), evaluating the identical Love/Shida numbers, Doodson/argument tables, and leap-second table.
- It keeps the permanent (mean) tide deformation: the original routine’s commented-out “Step 3” permanent-tide removal is left disabled, matching the ITRF/IGS conform-to-mean-tide convention.
- The routine names are changed from the IERS originals (per the IERS Conventions Software License), and the Fortran subroutine structure is inlined into private helpers.

The Sun and Moon geocentric positions are inputs (metres, ECEF/ITRF); the
caller supplies them, e.g. from [ crate::astro::bodies::sun_moon_ecef](https://docs.rs/astro/bodies/sun_moon/fn.sun_moon_ecef.html).

IERS Conventions Software License: permission is granted to use this software for any purpose, including commercial applications, free of charge, and to distribute derived works subject to the conditions reproduced above. Results obtained with this software acknowledge use of the IERS Conventions software.

- Per-station ocean-loading BLQ coefficients (Bos-Scherneck / HARDISP format).

# GnssSatelliteId in sidereon_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sidereon-core/0.11.0/sidereon_core/struct.GnssSatelliteId.html

pub struct GnssSatelliteId {
    pub system:
```
[GnssSystem](https://docs.rs/enum.GnssSystem.html),

}## Expand description

A satellite identifier: a constellation plus its within-system PRN/slot.

This is the `GnssSatelliteId { system, prn }` foundational type from the
spec (line 112). The `prn` is the within-constellation satellite number as
it appears in the product (e.g. the `01` in the SP3/RINEX token `G01`); it
is only meaningful in combination with [ GnssSatelliteId::system](https://docs.rs/struct.GnssSatelliteId.html#structfield.system).

`prn: `[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)The within-constellation PRN / slot number (e.g. `1` for `G01`).

# GnssSystem in sidereon_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sidereon-core/0.11.0/sidereon_core/enum.GnssSystem.html

```
pub enum GnssSystem {
    Gps,
    Glonass,
    Galileo,
    BeiDou,
    Qzss,
    Navic,
    Sbas,
}
```
## Expand description

A GNSS constellation (satellite system).

Variants follow the RINEX / IGS single-letter system identifiers, which are the canonical keys used throughout SP3, RINEX, and IONEX products:

| Letter | Variant | System |
|---|---|---|
| `G` | `GnssSystem::Gps` | GPS (US) |
| `R` | `GnssSystem::Glonass` | GLONASS (RU) |
| `E` | `GnssSystem::Galileo` | Galileo (EU) |
| `C` | `GnssSystem::BeiDou` | BeiDou (CN) |
| `J` | `GnssSystem::Qzss` | QZSS (JP) |
| `I` | `GnssSystem::Navic` | NavIC / IRNSS (IN) |
| `S` | `GnssSystem::Sbas` | SBAS (geostationary augmentation) |

Note that timekeeping is constellation-tagged separately (`TimeScale`):
GPS/Galileo/BeiDou each run their own system time, and GNSS week numbers are
**not** cross-comparable between systems.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

### Glonass

GLONASS (Russia), RINEX letter `R`.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.BeiDou)

### BeiDou

BeiDou (China), RINEX letter `C`.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Qzss)

### Qzss

QZSS (Japan), RINEX letter `J`.

NavIC / IRNSS (India), RINEX letter `I`.
